title: NIPT (non-invasive prenatal test)
what: Blood is taken from the mother's vein. It contains the baby's DNA, which is used to estimate the risk of some chromosome conditions.
why: Usually from 10 weeks of pregnancy, to estimate the risk of Down syndrome and other chromosome conditions, especially if screening showed a high risk.
duration: the blood draw takes 3 to 5 minutes; results usually come in 7 to 14 days
tell_doctor: Exactly how far along you are
If you are carrying twins or conceived through IVF
If you had a blood transfusion or an organ transplant
If genetic conditions run in your family

prepare.title: Timing
prepare.text: Usually done no earlier than 10 weeks. Your doctor or clinic will tell you when.

prepare.title: Food
prepare.text: Usually no fasting is needed. Check with the clinic.

prepare.title: Clothing
prepare.text: Wear a sleeve that is easy to roll up above the elbow.

bring: Ultrasound results showing how far along you are
steps: You fill out a form: weeks of pregnancy, height, weight, and pregnancy details
You sit down and rest your arm on the armrest
A band is tightened above your elbow, and the skin is wiped
Blood is drawn into a special tube
The needle comes out, and a cotton pad is pressed on
feel: A quick prick, like a pinch
The test is safe for the baby. Blood is taken only from the mother
after: Press the cotton pad for 3 to 5 minutes
Results usually come in 7 to 14 days
If the risk is high, your doctor will offer more tests. NIPT is not a final diagnosis

faq.a: No. Only the mother's blood is taken from a vein, like a regular test.

faq.q: If NIPT is fine, can I skip the ultrasound screening?
faq.a: No. The ultrasound shows something else: how the organs are developing. Your doctor usually orders both.

faq.q: Can I find out the baby's sex?
faq.a: Many tests show it. Ask the clinic if you want to know.

reminders.text: NIPT tomorrow. Bring your ultrasound results showing how far along you are.
